body.heading: The rules of the week
paragraphs: For seven days, send one thank-you a day — a message is fine — to seven different people, for seven specific things. Small is required: the colleague who always holds the lift, the friend whose laugh carried a bad week, the neighbour whose hedge makes the street prettier. Grand thanks are easy to postpone; small thanks fit in a Tuesday.
Specifics are the whole game. “Thanks for the playlist — the third song got me through the drive” is the unit you are aiming for.

body.heading: What tends to happen
paragraphs: Two things, reliably. First, people reply in a way that tells you your thanks arrived at exactly the right address — the small, unthanked efforts are precisely the ones people were quietly wondering whether anyone saw. Second, your own attention recalibrates: by day four you are scanning the day for thankable things, which is a pleasant way to move through the world.
Some people find a day surprisingly hard to fill. That is not failure; it is the experiment showing you where your gratitude has been running on autopilot.

body.heading: After the week
paragraphs: You do not need to keep a daily quota — quotas sour good things. Keep the scanning. A weekly thank-you, sent when spotted, maintains the muscle at a weight ordinary life can carry.
And if one of your seven replies with thanks of their own, you will have witnessed the whole mechanism: gratitude is the only gift that reliably generates more of itself.

takeaway: Seven days, seven specific thank-yous: small enough to send, large enough to recalibrate your attention.
